KEY MESSAGE 1...

With the upper level disturbance now to our east, mainly dry 
conditions are expected through the rest of the afternoon and 
evening outside of a few isolated showers lingering in the ADKs, 
however KENX radar shows most have passed to our west already. 
Clouds are expected to persist with current GOES satellite imagery 
showing a continuous layer of stratocumulus covering much of the 
region. Areas south in the Mid-Hudson Valley could see some breaks 
in the clouds allowing temperatures to warm up into the mid to upper 
70s, while the rest of the region stays cloudy and in the 50s and 
60s. Westerly winds will be breezy through the evening, especially 
channeled down the Mohawk Valley corridor into the Capital 
Region and Berkshires with gusts near 25 mph. Gradual clearing 
is expected overnight tonight as a high pressure system begins 
to build in from Eastern Ontario and the Great Lakes region, 
tracking overhead by tomorrow morning. With dewpoints dropping 
into the 30s and 40s, tomorrow will be a dry and pleasant day 
with highs in the mid 50s (terrain) and low 60s (valleys), along
with a light breeze and mostly sunny skies.

A strong upper level trough and associated frontal system will 
approach from the Great Lakes region tomorrow night into Friday, 
along with a progressive low pressure developing over the region 
Friday, tracking off the northern New England coast by Friday night. 
This will bring periods of stratiform rain showers starting just 
before sunrise Friday morning and remaining steady throughout most 
of Friday as the system's warm front passes through. A brief period 
of dry weather could occur in the afternoon, but additional 
scattered showers are expected late afternoon and into the evening 
as the system's cold front then passes through before tapering off 
into Saturday morning.

Model and ensemble guidance show PWATs being in the 1 to 1.5" range 
+1 to 2" STDEV above normal and above the climatological 75th 
percentile. Widespread rainfall totals of 1 to 2" are expected with 
the higher totals north of I-90 in the southern ADKs, southern Green 
mountains, and the Berkshire mountains, and the lower amounts in 
areas I-90 south. Some elevated instability could even allow for a 
few thunderstorms to develop Friday morning through afternoon. 
Sufficient bulk shear of 60 kt exists across the region, however 
there is still some uncertainty as to the exact locations of storms 
since CAMs and long range models show locations of greatest MUCAPE 
(600 J/kg) in areas south of I-90, and locations of steepest lapse 
rates (>6.5 C/km) and best synoptic forcing over the southern 
ADKs and western Mohawk Valley. There is a medium chance for 
thunderstorms across the region, but the chance for storms to 
become strong is low at this time. However, with this chance, 
there is the potential for brief heavy downpours and small hail.
NBM probabilistic guidance has a 60 to 80% chance of exceeding 
1.5" and a 30 to 40% chance of exceeding 2" for areas north of 
I-90 and a 20 to 40% chance of exceeding 1.5" south of I-90. 
With these totals falling over a longer duration, this looks to 
be another beneficial rainfall across much of the region. 
Flooding is not expected outside of some ponding of water in the
typical places of poor drainage and urban areas. Friday's highs
will be in the upper 50s (terrain) and upper 60s to approaching
the low 70s (valleys).

Temperatures turn chilly Friday night as the cold front passes 
through with most of the higher elevations falling below freezing 
and valleys dropping into the mid 30s by daybreak Saturday. The 
upper level trough axis will be centered over the region by Saturday 
morning with 850 hpa temps dropping down to around -8 to -10 C, 
which is well below normal for mid October. As a result, daytime 
temps will only be in the 30s across the high terrain on Saturday, 
with 40s for valley areas. In addition, a strong pressure gradient 
will result in breezy to gusty conditions, making it feel even 
colder through the weekend and making for a blustery late fall day. 
Steep low level lapse rates seen on forecast soundings amid a 
strong low level jet could help mix down strong wind gusts on 
Saturday. Probabilistic guidance has a 30-50% chance for gusts 
exceeding 40 mph within portions of the Mohawk Valley, Capital 
Region, Berkshires and eastern Catskills late Friday night 
through early Saturday afternoon which could approach wind 
advisory range and knock down foliated trees and blow around any
unsecured outdoors objects.

Although moisture will be limited behind the cold front, some lake 
enhanced and upslope precip may occur behind the front, allowing for 
some snow showers for western, northern and high terrain areas early 
Saturday morning. While some snowflakes do look likely across the 
higher terrain this weekend, total amounts look very minor at this 
time. Also, can not rule out some flurries extending into the 
eastern Mohaw
